Surah 91 "al-Shams" (The Sun) is Meccan by consensus, and it has fifteen verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ (1)

Mujahid said: "wa-duhaha" means its light and its shining. This is a second oath. He attributed the duha (forenoon brightness) to the sun, because it occurs when the sun has risen. Qatadah said: its brilliance. As-Suddi said: its heat. Ad-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding "wa-duhaha," that he said: He placed light in it and made it hot. Al-Yazidi said: it is its spreading out. It has also been said: it refers to everything created that becomes visible by it, so the oath is by the sun and by all the creatures of the earth. This was related by al-Mawardi. Ad-duha (al-Duha) is feminine. It is said: "irtafa'at al-duha" (the forenoon rose), and it is above al-dahw (the early morning). It may also be masculine. Whoever makes it feminine regards it as the plural of dahwa (ضَحْوَة). Whoever makes it masculine regards it as a noun in the pattern fu'l, like surad and nughar (names of small birds). It is an adverbial noun of time that is not fully declinable, like saharin (before dawn). You say: "laqituhu duhan wa-duha" (I met him in the forenoon), and if you mean the forenoon of your day, you do not add tanwin to it. Al-Farra' said: al-duha is the daytime, in the view of Qatadah. What is known among the Arabs is that al-duha is when the sun has risen and a little time has passed after that; when it increases, it is called al-duha' with a long vowel. Whoever says that al-duha is the entire day does so because the sun's light persists. Whoever says it is the sun's light or its heat, then the sun's light occurs only together with the sun's heat. Those who hold that al-duha is the sun's heat have cited the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿nor be exposed to the sun's heat﴾ [Ta-Ha: 119], meaning the heat does not harm you. Al-Mubarrad said: the root of al-duha is from ad-dihh, which is the light of the sun, and the alif is transposed from the second ha'. You say: dahwah and dahawat, and dahawat and duha. So the waw in (dahwa) is transposed from the second ha', and the alif in (duha) is transposed from the waw. Abu al-Haytham said: ad-dihh is the opposite of shade, which is the sunlight on the surface of the earth; its origin is ad-duha, but they found the yā' with a sukun on the ha' burdensome, so they changed it into an alif.

["And the moon when it follows it"] — meaning: it follows it. That is when it appears after the sun sets, at the crescent (al-hilal). It is said: "talawtu fulanan" (I followed so-and-so) when I followed him. Qatadah said: "That is only on the night of the crescent, when the moon appears (ra'a) after the sun sets." (Original note: the root is (ra'a); the yā' was placed before the hamzah.) Ibn Zayd said: "When the sun sets in the first half of the month, the moon follows it by rising; and at the end of the month it follows it by setting." Al-Farra' said: "talaha" means he took from it, going to the view that the moon takes from the light of the sun. Some people said: "And the moon when it follows it" means when it becomes full and round, so it was like it in brightness and light, and this was said by al-Zajjaj.

And by the day when it reveals it (3). That is, it uncovers it.

Some said: it reveals the darkness, even though no mention of it has preceded, just as you say, "Our morning became cold," meaning "our morning became cold." This is the view of al-Farra' (al-Farra') and al-Kalbi and others.

Others said: the pronoun in jallaha refers to the sun, and the meaning is that by its light it makes its body (jirm) clear. From this is the verse of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"She appeared to us like the sun beneath a cloud; a part of her edge showed, and she withheld the rest of her edge."

It was also said: it reveals what is on the earth of its living creatures until it becomes visible, since they are hidden at night and spread out by day. It was also said: it reveals the world. It was also said: it reveals the earth, even though no mention of it has preceded; and similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until it was hidden behind the veil﴾ [Sad 38:32], as was mentioned previously.

﴿By the night when it covers it﴾ (4). That is, it covers the sun, so that when the sun sets, the night takes away its light. This is said by Mujahid and others. It was also said: it covers the world with darkness, so the horizons become dark. So the pronoun ("it") refers to something not previously mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 91, verse 5:

﴿وَالسَّمَاءِ وَمَا بَنَاهَا﴾ (5). That is: "and its building." So "mā" is a verbal-noun particle (mā maṣdariyyah), as in His saying: ﴿بِمَا غَفَرَ لِي رَبِّي﴾ [Yasin: 27], meaning: "by the forgiveness of my Lord." This is the view of Qatadah, and al-Mubarrad preferred it.

It was also said: the meaning is "and He who built it" (man, "who"). This was said by al-Hasan and Mujahid, and it is the view preferred by al-Tabari; that is, "and He who created it and raised it up," and this is Allah, exalted is He.

It is related from the people of the Hijaz: "Glory be to what I glorify Him with," meaning: "Glory be to Him whom I glorify."

And the earth and He who spread it out (wa-ma ṭahāhā). Its literal sense: "wa-ṭaḥwihā," i.e., and its spreading out. It was also said: "wa-man ṭaḥāhā," meaning "He who spread it out," as we mentioned just above; that is, He spread it out. This is what most of the exegetes said, similar to "daḥāhā" (He spread it out).

Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and others said: ṭaḥāhā and daḥāhā are one and the same, meaning He spread it out from every side. Al-Ṭaḥw means spreading out: ṭaḥā yaṭḥū ṭaḥwan, and ṭaḥā yaṭḥā ṭaḥyan, and ṭuḥiyat, meaning she lay down (ḍṭaja'at), according to Abu 'Amr. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: ṭaḥāhā means He divided it (qasamahā). It was also said: He created it. The poet said:

"And Jadhima does not know who spread it out, nor who dwells on the lofty Throne."

Al-Mawardi said: It may also refer to what comes forth from it of plants, springs and treasures, because it is life for what He created upon it. It is said in some Arab oaths: "No, by the spreading moon (al-qamar al-ṭāḥī)," meaning the elevated, high-rising one. Abu 'Amr said: ṭaḥā al-rajul means when a man went off across the land. It is said: "I do not know where he went off (ṭaḥā)!" It is also said: ṭaḥā bihi qalbuhu, meaning his heart carried him off in every direction. 'Alqama said:

"Your heart was carried off toward the fair women, ardent in longing, far from youth, when gray hair has come."

It is said: the meaning is "and its fashioning." Here "ma" (in "wa-ma sawwaha") is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar). It is also said: the meaning is "and He who fashioned it," which is Allah, mighty and majestic. Regarding "al-nafs" (the soul) there are two opinions: the first is that it refers to Adam; the second is that it refers to every created soul. "Sawwa" is in the sense of "hayya'a" (prepared, arranged). Mujahid said: "sawwaha" means He perfected its creation and balanced it. All these names are in the genitive case as objects of the oath: Allah, exalted is His praise, swore by His creation because of the wondrous craftsmanship in it that points to Him.

Qur'anic verse: His saying, the Exalted: "fa-alhamahā" (﴿And He inspired it﴾), meaning He made it know (ʿarrafahā). Thus Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid. That is, He made it know the path of wickedness (fujur) and of God-consciousness (taqwa). Ibn ʿAbbas said the same. Also from Mujahid: He made it know obedience and disobedience. From Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, who said: "When God, Mighty and Majestic, wills good for His servant, He inspires him with good and he acts upon it; and when He wills evil for him, He inspires him with evil and he acts upon it." Al-Farra' said: "fa-alhamahā" – He made it know the path of good and the path of evil, as in His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two highways﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. Al-Dahhak related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "He inspired the believer who is God-conscious with his taqwa, and inspired the wicked with his fujur." From Saʿid, from Qatada, who said: "He made clear to it its wickedness and its God-consciousness." The meanings are close. It is narrated from Abu Hurayra that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited ﴿fa-alhamahā fujūrahā wa-taqwāhā﴾ and said: [O God, grant my soul its God-consciousness, and purify it, for You are the best to purify it; You are its Guardian and its Master.] Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Prophet (ﷺ), whenever he recited this verse, ﴿fa-alhamahā fujūrahā wa-taqwāhā﴾, raised his voice with it and said: [O God, grant my soul its God-consciousness; You are its Guardian and its Master, and You are the best to purify it.]

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, who said: ʿImran ibn Husayn said to me: "Do you see what people do today and strive at, is it a matter decreed and carried out upon them from a predestination that preceded, or is it concerning what they face from what their Prophet brought them, and the proof has been established against them?" I said: "Rather, it is a matter decreed upon them and carried out upon them." He said: "Then is it not injustice?" He said: "I was alarmed by that with great alarm, and I said: 'Everything is the creation of God and the possession of His hand; He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.'" He said to me: "May God have mercy on you! I only intended by what I asked you to test (uḥriza) your intellect: Two men of Muzayna came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of God, do you see what people do today and strive at: is it a matter decreed upon them and carried out upon them from a predestination that preceded, or is it concerning what they face from what their Prophet brought them, and the proof has been established against them?' He said: '(No, rather it is a matter decreed upon them and carried out upon them.) And the confirmation of that is in the Book of God, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And by a soul and Him who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its God-consciousness﴾.'"

The words fujūr and taqwā are both verbal nouns (maṣdar) functioning in the position of the direct object.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 91, verses 9–10:**

Allah's words: ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾. This is the answer to the oath, meaning: "Indeed, he has succeeded." Al-Zajjaj said: the lam (of emphasis) was dropped, because the speech was long, so its length became a substitute for it. It was also said: the answer is omitted, meaning "By the sun and its brightness, and so-and-so, you will surely be resurrected." Al-Zamakhshari said: its implied answer is ﴿Allah will surely destroy them﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, for their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), just as He destroyed Thamud, because they denied Salih. As for ﴿He has indeed succeeded who purifies it﴾, it is a statement that follows its opening, in view of His words ﴿And inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾, by way of digression (istitrad), and it is not part of the answer to the oath at all. It was also said: it is in the order of inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) without omission, and the meaning is: "He has indeed succeeded who purifies it, and he has indeed failed who corrupts it, by the sun and its brightness." Aflaha means he prevailed. "Who purifies it" means who purifies his soul through obedience.

﴿And he has failed who corrupts it﴾: that is, a soul has lost which Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has corrupted through disobedience. Ibn Abbas said: "A soul has failed which He has led astray and made deluded." It was also said: "He has succeeded who purifies his soul through obedience to Allah and righteous deeds, and he has failed who corrupts his soul with sins," said Qatadah and others.

The original meaning of zakat is growth and increase, and from it comes "zaka al-zar' (the crop grew)" when its yield increased. From it also comes the judge's "tazkiyah" of a witness, because he raises him by vouching for his integrity and mentioning his good qualities. This meaning has already been fully discussed at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, p. 343, second or third edition.]]. Thus the one who does good (mustani' al-ma'ruf) and hastens to righteous deeds makes his name famous and elevates himself. The noble Arabs used to descend to elevated and high ground so that their place would become known to those seeking gifts [[al-mu'tafi: everyone seeking bounty or provision.]], and they would kindle fire at night for the night-visitors. The base (al-lima') used to descend to caves, hollows and low valleys [[al-awlaj: what is a cave or grotto to which one takes refuge. al-ahdam: the lowest parts of valleys.]], so that their place would remain hidden from those seeking them. Thus the former exalted their souls and purified them, while the latter concealed their souls and corrupted them. Likewise, the wicked person is always hidden in place, scant in manliness (zamir al-muru'ah) [[al-zamir: few, scarce.]], obscure in person, and bowed-headed through committing sins.

It was also said: "dassaha" means "aghwaha" (led it astray). A poet said:

*"You are the one who led Amr astray, so that his wives became widows, ruined,"*

[[The verse in al-Lisan (root d-s-a) reads:

"And you are the one who led Amr astray, so that their women among them became widows, ruined."

He said: "dassayta" means "aghwayta" (you led astray) and "afsadta" (you corrupted). Amr is a tribe.]]

The people of language said: the original form is "dassasaha," from tadsis, which is concealing a thing within another thing. Its second sin was changed to a ya', as one says "qassaytu azfari" (I cut my nails), whose original is "qassastu azfari." Similar to this is their saying "taqaddada" in "taqaddada" becoming "taqadda." Ibn al-A'rabi said: "And he has failed who corrupts it" means he has inserted himself among the righteous while he is not one of them.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 91, verses 11–14:**

God's words: ﴿Thamud denied [their prophet] in their rebelliousness﴾. That is, in their *tughyan* (transgression, meaning their going beyond the limit in disobedience). This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah and others. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that *bi-taghwaha* means "by their punishment with which they had been threatened." He said: the name of the punishment that came upon them was *al-Taghwa*, because it overwhelmed them (*taghā ʿalayhim*). Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: *bi-taghwaha* means "all of them together." It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) and came in this form because it fits the rhyme of the verse endings (*ru'us al-ayy*). It has also been said that the original form is *bi-taghyaha*, but when the *fa'la* pattern comes from a root with a *ya'* (*dhawat al-ya'*), the *ya'* is changed to a *waw* in the noun, to distinguish the noun from the adjective. The common reading is with a *fatha* on the *ta'*. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari and Hammad ibn Salamah read it with a *damma* on the *ta'* (*bi-ḍammi al-ṭā'*), treating it as a verbal noun, like *al-ruj'a* and *al-husna* and similar verbal nouns. It has also been said that both are dialectal variants.

﴿When the most wretched of them rose up﴾: that is, stood up (*nahada*).

﴿The most wretched of them﴾: for slaughtering the she-camel. Her slaughterer's name was Qidar ibn Salif. What was said in *al-A'raf* [[See vol. 7, p. 241]] has already explained this, and whether he was one man or a group. In al-Bukhari, it is reported from 'Abdullah ibn Zam'ah that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) giving a sermon, in which he mentioned the she-camel and the one who slaughtered her. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When the most wretched of them rose up, a mighty man rose up for her, powerful, fierce [[al-'arim: the tyrannical, corrupting, savage one]], protected by his tribe, like Abu Zam'ah." He then mentioned the hadith. Muslim also transmitted it. Al-Dahhak also reported from 'Ali that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Do you know who was the most wretched of the first people?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "The slaughterer of the she-camel." He said: "Do you know who is the most wretched of the later people?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "The one who will kill you."

﴿Said to them the Messenger of God﴾: meaning Salih.

﴿The she-camel of God﴾: *nāqata* is in the accusative as a warning, like your saying "the lion, the lion," "the child, the child," or "beware, beware," meaning: beware of the she-camel of God, that is, of slaughtering her. It has also been said that the meaning is: leave the she-camel of God alone, as He said: ﴿This is the she-camel of God, a sign for you; so leave her to eat in God's land, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you﴾ [[Verse 73 of Surah al-A'raf]] [al-A'raf: 73].

﴿And her drink﴾: that is, leave her and her drinking. This has already been explained in Surah *al-Shu'ara'* [[See vol. 13, p. 131]], praise be to God, and also in Surah *Iqtarabat al-Sa'ah* [[See vol. 17, p. 141]] [al-Qamar: 1]. When they demanded the she-camel, and He brought her out for them from the rock, He made for them a day's share of water from their well, and for her a day's share in its place. This was hard on them.

﴿But they denied him﴾: that is, they denied Salih, peace be upon him, in his saying to them: "You will be punished if you slaughter her."

﴿Then they hamstrung her﴾: that is, the most wretched of them hamstrung her. The act was attributed to all of them because they were content with his deed. Qatadah said: we were told that he did not hamstring her until all of them, young and old, males and females, joined him in it. Al-Farra' said: two people hamstrung her. The Arabs say: "These two are the best of people," "These two are the best of people," and "This woman is the most wretched of the people," and therefore He did not say "the two most wretched of them" (*ashqayāhā*).

God's words: ﴿So their Lord crushed them over their sin﴾: that is, He destroyed them, and the punishment closed over them because of their sin, which is disbelief, denial and hamstringing. Al-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: *damdama 'alayhim* means "their Lord destroyed them over their sin," that is, over their crime. Al-Farra' said: *damdama* means "shook" (*arjafa*). The real meaning of *al-damdamah* is to intensify the punishment and repeat it. It is said: "I *dammamtu* over the thing," meaning I closed over it, and "dammam over him the grave," meaning he closed it over him. A "*mudammamah*" she-camel is one who has been clothed in fat. When you repeat the closing, you say *dammamtu*. And *al-damdamah* is destruction by uprooting, as al-Mu'arrij said. In *al-Sihah* it says: "I *dammamtu* the thing" means I stuck it to the ground and crushed it, and "God *dammama* over them" means He destroyed them. Al-Qushayri said: it has also been said, "I *dammamtu* the soil over the dead person," meaning I smoothed it over him. So His saying *dammama 'alayhim* means He destroyed them and placed them beneath the soil.

﴿And levelled it﴾: that is, He levelled the earth over them. According to the first interpretation, ﴿and levelled it﴾ means He levelled the crushing and the destruction over them, because the Cry destroyed them, and it reached their young and old alike. Ibn al-Anbari said: *dammama* means "became angry," and *al-damdamah* is speech that disturbs a man. Some lexicographers said: *al-damdamah* is "continuance" (*al-idamah*); the Arabs say a she-camel is *mudammamah*, meaning fat. It has also been said: ﴿and levelled it﴾ means He levelled the nation in bringing down the punishment upon them, young and old, lowly and noble, male and female. Ibn al-Zubayr read *fa-dammama*, and both are dialectal variants, as one says *imtaqa'a lawnuhu* and *intaqa'a* ("his color changed").

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And He does not fear its consequence.﴾ (15)

That is, God did this to them, [being] one who does not fear that any retribution for the destruction would fall upon Him from anyone. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and Mujahid. The pronoun in ʿuqbāhā (its consequence) refers to the deed (al-fiʿlah), as in His saying: "Whoever bathes on Friday, then with it [is good] and it is excellent" (fa-bihā wa-niʿmat), meaning: by the deed and the characteristic (al-khaṣlah). Al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi said: it refers to the one who hamstrung her (al-ʿāqir), meaning: the one who hamstrung her did not fear the consequence of what he did. Ibn 'Abbas also said this.

In the sentence there is inversion (taqdim wa-ta'khir); its implied meaning is: "When the most wretched of them was roused, and he does not fear its consequence." It has also been said: the Messenger of God Salih did not fear the consequence of the destruction of his people, nor did he fear any harm returning to him from their punishment, because he had warned them and God, may He be exalted, saved him when He destroyed them.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "fa-lā" with the fa' (fa-lā yakhāfu), and this is the more preferred reading, because it returns to the first meaning, i.e., "so He does not fear the consequence of their destruction." The rest [of the readers] read it with the waw (wa-lā yakhāfu), and this reading is more akin to the second meaning, i.e., "and the disbeliever does not fear the consequence of what he did."

Ibn Wahb and Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Malik, who said: Malik brought out to us a copy of the Mushaf that belonged to his grandfather, and he claimed that he had written it in the days of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan when he wrote the Mushafs, and in it was: "wa-lā yakhāfu" with the waw. Likewise it is so in the Mushafs of the people of Mecca and the Iraqis, with the waw; and Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this, following their Mushaf.
